datasets.datasetName: Published Results
datasets.experimentTitle: Influence of Weightlessness Upon Human Autonomic Cardiovascular Control
parameters: Carotid baroreflex, R-R interval at each carotid distending pressure
Carotid distending pressure, maximum R-R interval
Carotid distending pressure, minimum R-R interval
description:
Abstract: Although astronauts' cardiovascular function is normal while they are in space, many have altered haemodynamic responses to standing after they return to Earth, including inordinate tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, and uncommonly, syncope. Simulated microgravity impairs vagal baroreceptor-cardiac reflex function and causes orthostatic hypotension. Actual microgravity, however, has been shown to either increase, or not change vagal baroreflex gain. In this study, we tested the null hypothesis that spaceflight does not impair human baroreflex mechanisms. We studied 11 American and two German astronauts before, during (flight days 2-8), and after two, 9- and 10-day space shuttle missions, with graded neck pressure and suction, to elicit sigmoid, vagally mediated carotid baroreflex R-R interval responses. Baseline systolic pressures tended to be higher in space than on Earth (P = 0.015, repeated measures analysis of variance), and baseline R-R intervals tended to be lower (P = 0.049). Baroreceptor-cardiac reflex relations were displaced downward on the R-R interval axis in space. The average range of R-R interval responses to neck pressure changes declined from preflight levels by 37% on flight day 8 (P = 0.051), maximum R-R intervals declined by 14% (P = 0.003), and vagal baroreflex gain by 9% (P = 0.009). These measures returned to preflight levels by 7-10 days after astronauts returned to Earth. This study documents significant increases of arterial pressure and impairment of vagal baroreflex function in space. These results and results published earlier indicate that microgravity exposure augments sympathetic, and diminishes vagal cardiovascular influences.
Dwain L Eckberg, et al. J Physiol. 2010 April 1;588(Pt 7):1129-1138.

Supporting figures:
Figure 3. Mean ± 95% confidence intervals for preflight and inflight vagal baroreflex relations. From: Human vagal baroreflex mechanisms in space. Confidence limits for carotid distending pressures are obscured by the symbols. Open circles, preflight values; red circles inflight values.

Figure 4. Mean ± 95% confidence intervals for R–R interval changes provoked by baroreflex stimuli. From: Human vagal baroreflex mechanisms in space. Regressions for data from preflight to flight day 8 and from flight day 8 until postflight days 7–10 are shown with corresponding levels of significance. C, the integrals for all R–R interval responses to stimulus sequences. *Maximum R–R intervals during baroreflex testing were significantly lower on flight day 8 than preflight.

Figure 5. Mean ± 95% confidence intervals and individual (grey) vagal baroreflex gains for all subjects for all experimental sessions. From: Human vagal baroreflex mechanisms in space. Regression of baroreflex gains from preflight to flight day 8 was highly significant (P= 0.009). Individual data illustrate the great variability of vagal baroreflex gain among healthy subjects.

Figure 1. Baroreflex testing. From: Human vagal baroreflex mechanisms in space. The left panel shows astronaut Rhea Seddon performing baroreflex testing on herself during the SLS-1 mission. The custom-fabricated neck chamber was sealed around the mandible, posterior neck and chest with synthetic rubber. A, a stylized neck pressure sequence; B, R–R interval responses to the stimulus profile, telemetered from space; C, baroreceptor stimulus–R–R interval response relations for a different astronaut, studied preflight and on flight day 8 during the D-2 mission. In this and other figures, data from space are shown in red.

Figure 2. Mean (± 95% confidence limits) baseline arterial pressures and R–R intervals associated with each baroreflex test. From: Human vagal baroreflex mechanisms in space. Dashed lines indicate preflight averages. Results from repeated measures analysis of variance are given. The significance of pairwise differences was determined with the Holm–Sidak test. In panel B: *diastolic pressure was significantly higher on landing day than on all other experimental days. In panel C: *pulse pressure was significantly lower on flight day 8 than preflight, and **significantly higher on postflight day 4 than preflight, landing day, and postflight day 1. In panel D: *R–R intervals were significantly lower on flight day 8 than preflight.

datasets.datasetName: Final Report for Experiment 2.4.4
datasets.experimentTitle: Phenotypic and Functional Analysis of Peripheral Mononuclear Cells During Long Duration Space Flight
description:
This is the final report for this experiment. Sams CF, Konstantinova I, Meehan RT. Phenotypic and functional analysis of peripheral mononuclear cells during long duration space flight (STS-71 final research report). In: Shuttle-Mir Science Program Phase 1A Research Postflight Science Report. Houston, TX. Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center; 1998:1-55 - 1-60.

Data contained in the report:
Percentage of Lymphocytes on Mir 18: This graph represents the relative percentage of lymphocytes in circulating peripheral mononuclear cell populations collected from Mir 18 crewmembers. Data are expressed as a percentage of total leukocytes; each individual data bar represents an average three subjects. Samples were collected 150 and 35 days before launch, on flight day 11 of STS-71, on landing day, and nine days after recovery.

Percent of Granulocytes on Mir 18: This graph represents the percentage of granulocytes in circulating peripheral mononuclear cell populations collected from Mir 18 crewmembers. Data are expressed as a percentage of the total leukocyte count; each data bar represents and average of three subjects. Samples were collected 150 and 35 days before launch, on flight day 11 of STS-71, on landing day, and nine days after recovery.

Percent of Monocytes on Mir 18: This graph represents the percentage of monocytes in circulating peripheral mononuclear cell populations. Data are expressed as the percentage of total leukocytes; each data bar represents an average of three subjects. Samples were collected 150 days and 35 days before launch, on flight day 11 of STS-71, on landing day, and nine days after recovery.

Percent of Natural Killer Cells on Mir 18: This graph represents the percentage of natural killer cells in circulating peripheral mononuclear cell populations. Cells were identified as CD16/56 positive CD3 negative cells by flow cytometry. Data are expressed as the gated cell percentage of total lymphocytes. Samples were collected 150 and 35 days before launch, on flight day 11 of STS-71, on landing day, and nine days after recovery.

T-Cell Activation Response on Mir 18: This graph represents the T-cell activation response following 24 hour incubation with a lectin mitogen. Percentage of CD3+ cells (T-cells) expressing interleukin-2 receptors (CD25) was determined by flow cytometry. T-cell activation was carried out on cells isolated from blood samples collected on L-35 (35 days before launch of Mir 18), FD11 (Flight Day 11), R+0 (Landing Day of STS-71), and R+9.

T-Cell Activation Response on Mir 18: This graph represents the T-cell activation response following 24 hour incubation with a lectin mitogen. Percentage of CD3+ cells (T-cells) expressing CD69 markers was determined by flow cytometry. T-cell activation was carried out on cells isolated from blood samples collected on L-35 (35 days before launch of Mir 18), FD11 (Flight Day 11), R+0 (Landing Day of STS-71), and R+9.

datasets.datasetName: Spaceflight suppresses exercise-induced release of bioassayable growth hormone
datasets.experimentTitle: Relationship of Long-Term Electromyographic Activity and Hormonal Function to Muscle Atrophy and Performance
description:
This publication examines the effects of spaceflight on the hormonal responses (bioassayable growth hormone or BGH) to a unilateral plantar flexor exercise protocol. Four male astronauts on STS-78 (LMS) were examined. Data included are as follows:
  • Isometric plantar flexion exercise protocol
  • Plantar flexor torque and electromyographic activity of the soleus and medial gastrocnemius muscles during maximal voluntary contractions
  • Bioassayable and immunoassayable growth hormone (IGH and BGH)plasma concentrations before and after the exercise test
  • Immunoassayable IGF-I plasma concentrations preexercise and postexercise
  • Magnitudes of IGH and BGH exercise induced changes before, during, and after spaceflight

    Source: McCall GE, Goulet C, Roy RR, Grindeland RE, Boorman GI, Bigbee AJ, Hodgson JA, Greenisen MC, Edgerton VR. Spaceflight suppresses exercise-induced release of bioassayable growth hormone. J Appl Physiol 1999 Sep; 87(3):1207-12.

datasets.datasetName: Response of Serum Bone Formation Markers -- Osteocalcin and Bone Specific Alkaline Phosphatase L-1 to R+2
datasets.experimentTitle: Direct Measurement of the Initial Bone Response to Space Flight in Humans
description:
The graph shows the measured serum levels of Bone Specific Alkaline Phosphatase (BSAP) and Osteocalcin (OC). Both analytes are considered to be markers for overall turnover of bone under most circumstances, and which are thought to be more related to bone formation than to bone resorption. Space flight had no effect on BSAP. Osteocalcin was reduced for the first few days of flight, then increased back to baseline levels and remained there during flight and the first few days of recovery. This response is more consistent with a cause of stress of flight than of a bone response, although the bone response cannot be ruled out.

Source: Cann CE. Direct Measurement of the Initial Bone Response to Space Flight in Humans. Unpublished data: postflight one year status report to NASA.

datasets.datasetName: Final Report for Experiment 3.1.1
datasets.experimentTitle: Studies of Orthostatic Intolerance with the Use of LBNP
description:
This file contains the 30 day, 180 day, one year, and final report for the 3.1.1 study. The Mission Science Requirement Document (MSRD) is also attached. Data collection time tables are also included. Data represented in the final report:
Figure 1. Averaged Heart Rate data from preflight and inflight LBNP "ramp" tests on Shuttle (<15 days), Skylab (28-84 days) and Mir (110 days) crewmembers. It is apparent that all three groups are similar, both preflight and in flight at their respective test times.

Figure 2. Preflight, inflight, and postflight comparisons of Systolic, Diastolic, and Mean Arterial Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, Stroke Volume, and Total Peripheral Resistance at maximum decompression (-50 mmHg). There is a significant increase in Heart Rate from preflight to in flight (p=0.04) as was expected for the three Mir crewmembers (see *). There were no significant differences in any other parameters.

Figure 3. Measure of tolerance - Systolic, Diastolic, and Mean Arterial Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, Stroke Volume, and Total Peripheral Resistance are presented as the % change from 0-50 mmHg (control to maximum decompression). This figure illustrates the delta from baseline, thus factoring in the different endpoints for each crewmember and presenting the result as a group average. The change in Stroke Volume was significantly greater in flight and postflight compared to preflight (p=0.02) (see *). No other parameters exhibited a significant change, in part due to the large individual variability and small sample size. In fact, the statistical power for all of these comparisons should be considered when drawing any conclusions from these data.

datasets.datasetName: Effects of head-down-tilt bed rest on cerebral hemodynamics during orthostatic stress
datasets.experimentTitle: Integration of Neural Cardiovascular Control in Space
description:
Our aim was to determine whether the adaptation to simulated microgravity (microG) impairs regulation of cerebral blood flow (CBF) during orthostatic stress and contributes to orthostatic intolerance. Twelve healthy subjects (aged 24 +/- 5 yr) underwent 2 wk of -6 degrees head-down-tilt (HDT) bed rest to simulate hemodynamic changes that occur when humans are exposed to microG. CBF velocity in the middle cerebral artery (transcranial Doppler), blood pressure, cardiac output (acetylene rebreathing), and forearm blood flow were measured at each level of a ramped protocol of lower body negative pressure (LBNP; -15, -30, and -40 mmHg x 5 min, -50 mmHg x 3 min, then -10 mmHg every 3 min to presyncope) before and after bed rest. Orthostatic tolerance was assessed by using the cumulative stress index (CSI; mmHg x minutes) for the LBNP protocol. After bed rest, each individual's orthostatic tolerance was reduced, with the group CSI decreased by 24% associated with greater decreases in cardiac output and greater increases in systemic vascular resistance at each level of LBNP. Before bed rest, mean CBF velocity decreased by 14, 10, and 45% at -40 mmHg, -50 mmHg, and maximal LBNP, respectively. After bed rest, mean velocity decreased by 16% at -30 mmHg and by 21, 35, and 39% at -40 mmHg, -50 mmHg, and maximal LBNP, respectively. Compared with pre-bed rest, post-bed-rest mean velocity was less by 11, 10, and 21% at -30, -40, and -50 mmHg, respectively. However, there was no significant difference at maximal LBNP. We conclude that cerebral autoregulation during orthostatic stress is impaired by adaptation to simulated microG as evidenced by an earlier and greater fall in CBF velocity during LBNP. We speculate that impairment of cerebral autoregulation may contribute to the reduced orthostatic tolerance after bed rest.

Source: Zhang R, Zuckerman JH, Pawelczyk JA, Levine BD. Effects of head-down-tilt bed rest on cerebral hemodynamics during orthostatic stress. J Appl Physiol. 1997 Dec;83(6):2139-45.

datasets.datasetName: Insulin content in the head of the pancreas from STS-40
datasets.experimentTitle: Vitamin D Endocrine System After Short-term Spaceflight
parameters: In situ levels; Insulin, pancreas, rat
description: The concentration of insulin in the head of the pancreas from rats flown on STS-40 (SLS-1) tended to be lower than that of STS-58. The insulin concentration for flight animals from STS-40 “immediately” following recovery (F, R+0) was 103.9 +/-11.9 ng/mg (n=10), which was significantly greater (P < 0.02) than flight controls (C, R+0) 58.2 +/- 11.0 ng/mg (n=5). The insulin content of flight animals (F, R+0) was not significantly different from vivarium controls (CV, R+0), 84.9 +/- 9.4 ng/mg (n=5) or basal controls (L+0), 83.4 +/- 12.1 ng/mg (n=5). As with rats from the STS-54 flight, there was no difference between flight animals held for mission-length after recovery (F, R+ML), 97.9 +/- 14.2 ng/mg (n=9) and recovery plus mission-length control animals (C, R+ML: 67.4 +/- 16.3 ng/mg; CV, R+ML: 131.3 +/-9.3 ng/,g).

datasets.datasetName: Average Calbindin-D28k in Animal Groups from SLS-1 and SLS-2
datasets.experimentTitle: Vitamin D Endocrine System After Short-term Spaceflight
parameters: In situ levels; Calbindin, kidney, rat
description:
This spreadsheet shows average kidney calbindin-D28k levels in flight and control animals from SLS-1 and SLS-2.

The results of this study with ELISA of calbindin-D28k did not confirm the reduction in calbindn-D28k found in our earlier study (Sergeev, et al., 1996). Calbindin-D28k levels in kidneys of SLS-1 flight animals after just returning to Earth (R+0), 2.24 +/- 0.17 ug/mg protein, were significantly greater than those of basal controls (L+0), 0.89 +/- 0.06 ug/mg, but not ground controls (GC), 1.97 +/-0.03 (Figure 4). Levels of calbindin-D28k measured by ELISA were equivalent in flight animals immediately following flight (R+0) and after nine days at Earth gravity (R+ML), 1.94 +/- 0.12 ug/mg protein (P=0.5). In SLS-2 animals, renal calbindin-D28k in flight animals after just returning to Earth (R+0), 2.22 +/- 0.27 ug/mg protein, was significantly greater than basal controls (L+0), 1.08 +/- 0.13, (P<0.001) and ground controls, 0.62 +/- 0.04 (P<0.001) (Figure 5). Calbindin-D28k in kidneys of flight animals after return to Earth gravity (R+0) was similar to those of flight animals after 14 days at Earth gravity (R+ML), 2.03 +/- 0.11 (P=0.5) and to animals sacrificed in flight (FD13), 2.75 +/- 0.31 (P=0.06). Thus, the results of this study indicate an increase in calbindin-D28k levels in microgravity. Differences in the results of this and our previous study (Sergeev, et al., 1996) suggest that other factors the animals are exposed to during flight regulate in a substantial way calbindin-D28k. Among these factors may be environmental stresses, such as elevated temperatures (from about 24.5 C to 28.5 C in SLS-2) and reduced humidity (slightly more than 30% to over 100% for SLS-2). Temperature extremes were even greater for SLS-1 (27-32 C).

datasets.datasetName: NIH.R1 Feasibility Tests 1 and 2 and Procedures Validation Test (PVT) data
datasets.experimentTitle: Effects of Weightlessness on Vestibular Development
parameters: Size, length; Body, rat pup; Digitizer and PC
description:
This database contains information from the two Feasibility Tests and the Procedures Validation Test. The format is identical to the database generated for the NIH.R1 flight and contains information gathered during surgeries and following delivery of the pups. Several summaries can be generated from this file, including:
• laparotomies
• surgeries
• fetal survival
• fetus and pup weights
• resorptions

Please refer to list of scripts to see summaries that can be generated. All information on an animal by animal basis has been combined on one form, the Single Page Form, that can be used to see the complete picture. For a less complete summary by treatment group, see the Dam Data Summary.

Rodent maintenance information (body weight, food and water consumption) is compiled with the data books from each test. Data from the Procedures Validation Test was collected electronically via the Electronic Data Collection System (EDCS) in the FileMaker application.

datasets.datasetName: Number Recognition Task
datasets.experimentTitle: The Effects of Long-Duration Space Flight on Eye, Head, and Trunk Coordination During Locomotion
description:
This file contains an image depicting results from the number recognition task (DVA test) during walking at 6.4 km/h. Box plots show results for six NASA-Mir subjects. These results show a trend of diminished dynamic visual acuity after space flight and a recovery over the first week following return to Earth.

Source: Layne CS, Mulavara AP, McDonald PV, Kozlovskaya IB, and Bloomberg JJ. The effects of long-duration space flight on eye, head, and trunk coordination during locomotion. NASA 2 Final Research Paper. Houston, TX.

datasets.datasetName: Muscle Atrophy with Bed Rest
datasets.experimentTitle: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) after Exposure to Microgravity
description: This figure shows the published muscle atrophy results from horizontal bed rest.  Comparison of the flight data with bed rest shows that the changes in the leg muscles during flight were generally less than bed rest.  This is likely a consequence of the exercise countermeasure employed during flight since the bed rest data did not include exercise  Source: Unpublished data (PI final report to NASA.  Experiment E586-Magnetic Resonance Imaging After Exposure to Microgravity.  August 1, 1999.)

datasets.datasetName: Early Postflight Muscle Volume Percent Change from Baseline
datasets.experimentTitle: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) after Exposure to Microgravity
description: This table shows the muscle volume changes between R+0 and R+2-4 days after flight in four crewmembers.  This table demonstrates the muscle swelling that can occur during the early reambulation period which is also usually seen after bed rest.  The largest changes are in the calf, particularly the gastrocnemius.<END>

datasets.datasetName: Published data for Experiment 9401613
datasets.experimentTitle: Protein Metabolism During Long Term Space Flights
description:
Datasets available in Stein TP, Leskiw MJ. Oxidant damage during and after spaceflight. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2000 Mar;278(3):E375-82. This publication includes Mir data as well as LMS (STS-78) and bedrest data.

Mir data: The subjects for this study were two astronauts (American) and four cosmonauts (Russian).

Data in this publication:

  • Diet, and isoprostane [8-iso-prostaglandin F2a (8-iso-PGF2a)] and 8-oxo-7,8 dihydro-2 deoxyguanosine (8-OH DG) excretion before, during, and after spaceflight on MIR. Isoprostane data are for unextracted (UN) and extracted (EX) urine.
  • Antioxidant intakes before, during, and after spaceflight on MIR
  • Changes in unextracted (UN) and extracted (EX) isoprostane [8-iso-prostaglandin F2a (8-iso-PGF2a)] and 8-oxo-7,8 dihydro-2 deoxyguanosine (8-OH DG) excretion during and after spaceflight on MIR. There were 6 subjects. Data are expressed as percentage of mean preflight data normalized to creatinine.
  • Changes in UN isoprostane and 8-OH DG excretion during and after spaceflight on the shuttle.

datasets.datasetName: Passive Implanted Silicon (PIPS) Detector Data in Correlation to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) Data during a Solar Particle Event
datasets.experimentTitle: Active Dosimetry of Charged Particles
description: This figure shows the time profile of the count rate (counts per second) measured onboard the Mir Space Station during the November 6, 1997, solar particle event (top panel) and of protons measured on the NOAA GOES-satellite during the same time period (bottom panel).  A SPE also occurred on November 4, 1997, however the data were completely lost as shown by the absence of measurements in the left-most part of the top panel.  The data for the conclusion of the November 6 SPE were also lost.  However, during the onset of the November 6 event the Mir Space Station was in the optimal orbital position (i.e. lowest cutoff portions of the orbit) and therefore the measurements reflect the onset and the period of the highest SPE dose contribution. The obvious feature of the SPE event is the presence of high dose maxima at high north and south latitudes, which are comparable to the data experienced during South Atlantic Anomaly crossings. Source: Unpublished (PI final report to NASA).<END>

datasets.datasetName: Urinary values in placebo and potassium citrate-treated crewmembers
datasets.experimentTitle: Renal Stone Risk During Space Flight:  Assessment and Countermeasure Validation
description:

Graph A shows percent change in citrate from preflight during first 35 (E-FLT), 36 to 120 (M-FLT) and greater than 120 (L-FLT) spaceflight days. Asterisk indicates p<0.05. Graph B shows calcium excretion before (Pre), during and after long duration spaceflight. R+10, 10 to 18 days after landing. Asterisk indicates p<0.05 vs placebo.

PRE=preflight. E-FLT=first 35 spaceflight days. M-FLT= 36 to 120 spaceflight days. L-FLT=greater than 120 spaceflight days. R+10=10 to 18 days after landing.

Graph B, calculated CAOX stone risk in individuals. Relative CAOX supersaturation was significantly higher in placebo (open circles) than in KCIT (black circles) group (p=0.002). datasets.datasetName: Significant Twenty-four Hour Urine Biochemistry Changes
datasets.experimentTitle: Clinical Biochemistry
description:
The biochemical studies on Apollo varied somewhat between missions depending on overall mission objectives. In general, Apollo missions 7, 8, 9 , and 10 were supported in the same manner. Apollo 11, 12, and 14 were characterized by a postflight quarantine and therefore received similar laboratory emphasis. Apollo missions 15, 16, and 17 were supported with an expanded protocol characterized by an increasing number of biochemical studies. The general methods included the withdrawal of 20-ml of venous blood at least three times, approximately thirty, fifteen, and five days before each mission. Similar amounts of blood were withdrawn within two hours after recovery, one day, seven days, and fourteen days later. Fasting blood samples were obtained with the crewmember recumbent and at approximately the same time each day except for the sample immediately after splashdown.

The mean of preflight data for each flight (three crewmen, three sample dates) was obtained and the standard deviation of the mean calculated. The mean value of the postflight data (three crewmen, one sample date), the standard deviation and the percent deviation from the preflight level were recorded. The results were submitted to student’s paired t-test.

The following standard clinical biochemical laboratory techniques were used to perform the analyses:

Autoanalyzer: cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, inorganic phosphate, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, uric acid, urea nitrogen, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase
Flame photometry: sodium, potassium
Freezing point depression: osmolality
Atomic absorption: magnesium , calcium
Titration: chloride
Robot chemist: creatine phosphokinase, lactic dehydrogenase, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT)
Rare reaction analysis: creatine phosphokinase, lactic dehydrogenase, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase

Aliquots of twenty-four hour urine samples are analyzed for electrolytes, specific gravity, volume, creatinine, and uric acid. The overall mean value of each parameter is presented in a table as either having increased or decreased.
Source: Alexander WC, Leach CS, Fischer CL. Clinical biochemistry. In: Johnston RS, Dietlein LF, Berry CA, eds. Biomedical Results of Apollo. Washington, DC: National Aeronautics and Space Administration; 1975: 185-196. NASA Special Publication SP-368.

datasets.datasetName: Orthostatic Stress Procedure Protocol
datasets.experimentTitle: Apollo Flight Crew Cardiovascular Evaluations
description:
The protocols for the 2 orthostatic stress procedures are shown. The supine LBNP protocol consisted of a 5-minute resting control period, a 5-minute period at each of 3 distinct reduced-pressure levels, and a 5-minute recovery period. The first 5-minute period of reduced pressure included one minute at -8 mm Hg (-11 x 102 N/m2) ) and one minute at -16 mm Hg (-21 x 102 N/m2) ), followed by 3 minutes at -30 mm Hg (-40 x 102 N/m2) ). The 2 short-duration, relatively low levels of reduced pressure were adopted to obtain additional information regarding the responsiveness of lower limb capacitance vessels. The three levels of sequentially applied reduced pressure used were chosen on the basis of previous experience in the JSC Cardiovascular Laboratory (Wolthuis et al., 1970). As reported, the use of an incremental LBNP protocol produced physiological responses for each level of reduced pressure applied and ensured a measurable, quantitative stress response in both the normal preflight and the orthostatically intolerant postflight conditions. The passive stand protocol consisted of a 5-minute resting supine control period followed by a 5-minute passive stand. For the passive stand, the subject leaned against a wall in a relaxed manner with his heels spaced 15 cm (6 in.) away from the wall.

Source: Hoffler GW, Johnson RL. Apollo flight crew cardiovascular evaluations. In: Johnson RS, Dietlein LF, Berry CA, eds. Biomedical Results of Apollo. Washington, DC: NASA Headquarters; 1975:234-235. NASA SP-368.

datasets.datasetName: Rodent Research 2 (RR2) Environmental Monitoring Data
datasets.experimentTitle: Rodent Research 2 (RR2)
description:
This portion of Series I of the Rodent Research 2 data collection contains environmental monitoring data for the Rodent Research experiment on the International Space Station (ISS), and in associated ground controls at Kennedy Space Center.

The Flight_and_Ground directory contains environmental data collected for the habitat modules. Flight and ground telemetry subdirectories include temperature and humidity data, video and lighting status, and schedules. The data were logged as raw files (csv format), reduced data (csv format), and processed data. Descriptions of the data and how it was processed and analylzed are provided in "Read me" file in the directory.

The NRT_ListRequests subdirectory includes analysis of the flight data, including files with data retrieved through EHS NRT requests that were merged with Acquisition of Signal (AOS)/Loss of Signal (LOS) data from the entire mission. LOS was not an issue for the ground control habitats. Complete AOS/LOS data were only retrieved for the last few weeks of the mission. Rodent Habitat 2 (RH 2 , SN 209) and 4 (RH 4, SN 210) NRT requests used to generate these files were sampled at five-minute intervals.

datasets.datasetName: Integral Number Linear Energy Transfer (LET) Spectrum for Particles Found during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) and Skylab
datasets.experimentTitle: In-flight Radiation Detection
description:
This graph shows the integral number linear energy transfer (LET) spectrum for particles incident on ASTP and Skylab astronauts, the command module, and film vault. Cosmic-ray nuclei was also calculated in space and inside Skylab.

The integral number density of high-LET particles is plotted against the LET value. The integral LET spectrum measured in one ASTP dosimeter is shown in the graph. For comparison, spectra measured during Skylab and the Apollo 17 lunar mission, as well as calculated cosmic ray nuclei are also displayed.

datasets.datasetName: PSE.03 Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR) data for the two 48-hour delayed ground control Animal Enclosure Modules (AEM) located at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in the Orbital Environmental Simulator (OES)
datasets.experimentTitle: Effect of Weightlessness on Tissue Regeneration in Rodents
parameters: Temperature; AEM, PSE.03; Ambient temperature recorder (ATR)
description:
The datasets represent ATR-4 devices installed in 2 ground AEMs, housed in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator (OES) at KSC/CCAFS/Hangar L/2nd floor. These AEMs were set up on 6/21/93 (ATR-4 activation approximately 10:55am EDT 6/21/93), installed in the OES at approximately 1700h on 6/21/93, with simulated launch on 6/23/93, simulated landing on 7/3/93, and animals and ATR-4s removed on 7/3/93 (approximately 1200h) , in all cases on a strictly 48-hour delay basis as regards the flight AEMs.

Within each dataset are temperature measurement timepoints separated by 225 seconds (3.75 minutes). At each temperature measurement timepoint, there are 4 temperatures (in degrees C.), representing the internal temperature sensor in the ATR-4 (channel 1), and the 3 external probes attached to each ATR-4. In each data timepoint entry in the dataset, the data read (from left to right): time; channel 1, channel 2, channel 3, channel 4. For PSE.03, the ATR-4s were configured to record 4 channels of temperature data, with channel 1 recording from the ATR-4 internal temperature sensor, and the remaining 3 channels recording data from remotely-placed external temperature probes.

datasets.datasetName: Absorbed Doses at Dloc Locations by Passive Dosimeters
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This table shows the measured absorbed doses from the 7LiF mono crystals (TLDs) obtained at the same Dloc location in the Shuttle. The Russian hardware from the flight were returned to lBMP for processing. The measured doses are in excellent agreement, the root mean square error is 5.7% and the maximum difference is less than 10%.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Crew Absorbed Doses from Passive Dosimeters
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This table shows a comparison of absorbed doses from TLD passive dosimeters. Each crewmember wore one U.S. and one Russian passive dosimeter. There is very good overall agreement between the two sets of measurements. However, the remaining differences between measurements of about 7% may be due to the crewmembers storing their dosimeters in different locations.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Dloc 2 Dose Rates
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Estimated ISS Dose Rates as a Function of Altitude during Solar Minimum
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
The investigators used the measured quality factors of trapped and GCR particles in the core module to calculate the dose equivalent rate with altitude. The BFO dose and dose equivalent rates were calculated so that they were consistent with skin dose rate calculation. These are given in this graph.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: NASA-Mir Dose and Dose Equivalent Rates as Measured by TEPC
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This chart summarizes some of the measurements between the spectra arise due to shielding differences and to the east-west asymmetry of particle. As seen in this chart, the quality factor was the highest in the core module. It should be noted that it is unlikely that the International Space Station (ISS) will be operated at 470 km during solar minimum, a situation more likely to occur during solar maximum.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Integral LET Spectra from Various Mir Modules
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph shows the integral LET spectra of trapped particles in various modules of the Mir station. The differences between the spectra arise due to shielding differences and to the east-west asymmetry of particle fluxes.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79 (5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Trapped Dose Rate as a Function of Atmospheric Density
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
In order to better understand the dose rate data, the trapped particle dose rate at the six fixed locations (middeck and flight deck) from 28.5° inclination flights as a function of the atmospheric density is plotted in this graph. The density incorporates the variation of altitude and solar heating due to changing solar UV output. The minimum energy required to reach the dosimeter is given alongside as is the index of a power law fit to the density.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Plot of Trapped Dose Rate as a Function of Atmospheric Density
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This is a plot of the trapped dose rates as derived from the R-16 measurements, U.S. TEPC in the Spektr module, and the ESA Radiation Environment Monitor (REM), which is mounted on the outside of the Base Block, with atmospheric density.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Integrated Dose Rate
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph depicts the integrated dose rate as a function of the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) dose weighted altitude during STS-63 for the DSO 200 study. The dose rate behavior of this omnidirectional detector, except for the scale, is rather similar to that of the starboard AAD.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. Intercomparison of radiation measurements on STS-63. 1996.

datasets.datasetName: Average Cosmonaut Absorbed Dose and Dose Rates On Board the Mir Station
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This chart contains the average (Commander and Flight Engineer) cosmonaut radiation exposure for various Mir missions starting with the first mission on March 13, 1986. Other information pertinent to each mission is also given. The highest exposure of 8.70 µGy was seen during the Mir-22 mission. The following points about these data should be noted: (1) due to differences in the spacecraft shielding, one crew member gets about a factor two higher dose than the other; (2) TLDs have low efficiency for high LET particles and do not detect neutrons. Correcting for this loss would increase the total dose by about a factor of 1.25; (3) these rates are representatives of the dose rate in the Core Module (Base Block) of the Mir station, and other modules, such as the Kvant, have higher dose rates; and (4) there is an altitude variation of up to 30 km between the missions that significantly impacts the dose from the SAA.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Differential Neutron Energy Spectra from 28.5° Inclination Flights
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph shows the differential neutron energy spectra from four Shuttle flights. These spectra are converted into dose rates and dose equivalent rates and are given in Table 1 of the referenced publication.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Estimated GCR Dose Rate as a Function of Time
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
The estimated GCR dose rate as a function of time is plotted in this graph. The dose rate in the Base Block varies from a low of 40 µGy d-1 (solar maximum) and a high of 145 µGy d-1 (solar minimum). These rates are weakly dependent upon the station module shielding distribution. The uncertainty on this dose rate is estimated to be ± 15%.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate as a Function of Mission Elapsed Time
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph (lower panel) shows a plot of dose rate as a function of mission elapsed time. The dose rate changed from about 6 µGy min-1 for the first two days to about 2 µGy min-1 for the following two days and then returned to 6 µGy d-1. In the upper panel is a plot of the angle between the local magnetic field direction and the z body axis of the Shuttle. The correlation between the Shuttle altitude and dose rate is obvious. There is a factor of 2.7 between the dose rates from the two directions.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

description:
This graph depicts the dose rate measured by port side AAD as a function of mission elapsed time (MET) in minutes during STS-63 for the DSO 200 study.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. Intercomparison of radiation measurements on STS-63. 1996. Nov;26(6):901-16.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate Contour Plot of the SEP event of November 6-8, 1997
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
The solar particles are easily separable from both the GCR and trapped particles. The total additional dose and dose equivalent from the SEP was 0.156 mGy and 0.33 mSv respectively. This graph depicts a dose rate contour from this event and indicates that most of these particles were seen near the geomagnetic polar region, as expected; however, particles were seen down to 30° latitude, indicating that the event had GeV range particles.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate versus Time from November 6-8, 1998
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
The first event from the current 23rd cycle was observed during 6–8 November 1997 by the U.S. TEPC in the Priroda module on the Mir station. This is a plot of dose rate with time.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Neutron Dose and Dose Equivalent Rates in the Shuttle Middeck Locker
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This chart contains the differential neutron energy spectra from four Shuttle flights (STS-55, STS-57, STS-65 and STS-94), which were converted into dose rates and dose equivalent rates. Although the contribution to dose rate is small, the contribution to dose equivalent rate varied from 14–60% of the charged particle dose rate. If one adds the contribution of neutrons above 12 MeV, this would increase by another 15–25%, a significant component for long duration flights. Note that the average quality factor is 8–9.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Average Cosmonaut Dose Rate as a Function of the Mission Launch Date
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects

This is a plot of the dose rate as a function of time. It ranges from 182 to 397 µGyd-1.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Integrated Dose Rates and Altitude
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph depicts the ratio of the integrated dose rates as a function of the altitude. The ratio decreases from 2.8 to 1 and then reaches values of 1.5 to 1.6. The actual shape of the curve may also reflect the sampling statistics of the short period at each orbital altitude.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. Intercomparison of radiation measurements on STS-63. 1996. Nov;26(6):901-16.

datasets.datasetName: TEPC Measured Dose Rate as a Function of Longitude
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This is a plot of the TEPC measured dose rate (averaged over latitude) as a function of longitude in the SAA region and its comparison with model calculations. The longitude profile averaged over latitude from 10 to 50° S from TEPC and AP8 model, which are also plotted in the graph. The measured peak was shifted from the calculated peak westward by 6.4 ± 0.89°. This shift is slightly smaller than the 6.9 ± 0.82° measured on STS-31, which was in a 28.5° x 617 km altitude orbit.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Low-Energy Neutron Fluence
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This table shows low-energy neutron fluence and dose equivalent from area passive detectors in middeck locker (MF28H). The average dose equivalent from neutrons of energy less than 1 MeV is 2.53 ± 1.33 µSv/day.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Average Astronaut Dose Rate as a Function of Altitude
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
The average astronaut dose rate as a function of flight altitude for 28.5° and 57° inclination flights is plotted in this graph. Except for STS-28 that had a slight solar particle event (SPE) contribution, the dose comes from GCR and SAA particles. At low altitudes, the dose is dominated by GCR and at high altitudes by SAA particles. At about 400 km and solar minimum, the two contributions to the dose are roughly equal.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: TEPC Dose
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph depicts the measured absorbed dose rate and flight altitude as a function of mission elapsed time (MET). There were five clearly separated times during which the Shuttle flew at nearly constant, but increasing, altitude.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. Intercomparison of radiation measurements on STS-63. 1996. Nov;26(6):901-16.

datasets.datasetName: Measured GCR dose rate as a Function of Deceleration Potential
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph depicts the combined GCR dose rates measured by the U.S. tissue equivalent proportional counter (TEPC) from March 1995 to January 1998, with data acquired by the Liulin during the last solar cycle, and plotted as a function of the deceleration potential, f(MV). This potential is a parameter that incorporates the solar wind velocity, the interplanetary diffusion coefficient (and their radial dependence), and the extent of the heliospheric boundary from the point of observation. It can be more simply understood as a repulsive potential that cosmic ray particles from the interstellar space have to overcome to reach the point of observation.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Total Measured Absorbed Dose Rate as a Function of Time from the R-16 Dosimeters
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Solar Particle Events Observed on the Mir Station during the Twenty-Second Cycle
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This chart contains the list of events that resulted in an R-16 measured excess dose from the event of >0.01 cGy during the last 22nd solar cycle. Typically, the ratio of the dose at R-16 to dose in free space varied from a low of 8 X 3 10-3 to a high of 10<-3>.

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: Average LET and Quality Factor
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This table shows the average LET and Quaity Factor using high temperature TLD peak from IBMP area passive dosimeter at Dloc 2. The table also shows the average LET under 1 and 2 mm polystyrene and under 3 mm of aluminum. The values range from 1.62 to 2.94, with the TLD-600 values being always higher and clearly indicating the presence of low-energy neutrons. The flux of high LET particles resulting from the target fragmentations is very sensitive to the shielding very close to the detector and thus can have an impact on the average Quality Factor. This fact must be taken into consideration when comparing these measurements with those from other detectors.

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. In-flight radiation measurements on STS-60. 1996. Jan; 26(1):17-34.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate and Various Planetary Indices from the September-October 1989 Events
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph shows the sequence of events beginning in September 1989. Data of fluxes from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES), the Planetary Index, Kp,, and the Dst index as a function of time are also given. These indices give the strength of magnetic field disturbance that can and does lead to a lowering of the geomagnetic cutoff. During the September period the indices were relatively quiet and thus the cutoff values were representative of the quiescent field conditions (about 200 MeV).

Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

datasets.datasetName: TEPC Dose Rate Contour Plot
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Radiobiological Effects
description:
This graph depicts the latitude (- 51.65° to -10°) averaged dose rate as a function of longitude. The solid line is the fit through these data points, assuming the shape to be a gaussian plus a constant background dose rate. The peak dose rate from this fit is found to be at longitude ( - 41.1° ± 0.8°). This compares very well with the peak from STS-60 data (- 39.8° ± 0.51°).

Source: Badhwar GD, et al. Intercomparison of radiation measurements on STS-63. 1996. Nov;26(6):901-16.

datasets.datasetName: Percent Distribution of Spectral Power
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations:  Sensory-Motor Investigations (SMI)
description:
This graph depicts the percent distribution of spectral power for the three EGG frequency ranges of the gastric myoelectric activity. These three frequency ranges are bradygastria, which is 0.9 to 2.04 cycles per minute (cpm), tachygastria, which is 4.08 to 9.6 cpm and normogastria, which is 2.34 to 3.78 cpm. These three ranges are distinguished in the bars by differing shades of gray. The first two bar graphs show this information for two nausea events experienced by the same crewmember. The percent spectral power relating to 30 minutes and 15 minutes before nausea and 15 minutes, 30 minutes and 45 minutes after nausea are shown. The third bar graph shows the percent spectral power for the vomiting event of another crewmember. Again, 30 minutes and 15 minutes before vomiting and 15 minutes, 30 minutes and 45 minutes after vomiting are shown in the figure.

In the first episode of nausea, approximately 60% of the spectral power was associated with abnormal gastric rhythms before nausea was reported. Following the nausea report, the abnormal rhythms increased to approximately 75% of the spectral power then gradually decreased to approximately 45% at 45 minutes following the report.

The second episode of nausea gave a percent spectral power associated with abnormal rhythms that was 75 to 80% throughout the recording time of 30 minutes before nausea to 45 minutes after nausea. In this second nausea event, a higher percent spectral power was associated with the faster waves of tachygastria duing the time following the report, whereas in the first nausea event, the percent spectral power associated with the slower waves of bradygastria was two to three times greater than that of tachygastria.

For the vomiting episode, 75 to 80% of the spectral power was observed with abnormal gastric rhythms before and up to 30 minutes following the episode. The gastric myoelectric activity returned to normal by 45 minutes after the report with approximately 70% of the power in the normal gastric slow wave frequency range.

Source: Harm DL, Sandoz GR, Stern RM. Changes in Gastric Myoelectric Activity During Space Flight. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2002 Aug; 47(8):1737-1745.

datasets.datasetName: Running Spectra of the EGG for One of the Nausea Episodes
datasets.experimentTitle: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations:  Sensory-Motor Investigations (SMI)
description:
The running spectra of the EGG for one of the nausea episodes for 30 minutes before and 30 minutes following the report of nausea is shown. The minutes before nausea are shown as negative values and the minutes following the nausea are positive values. Each segment of the spectra overlaps the previous one by 75%, resulting in 51.2 seconds of new data in each segment. The spectra associated with the period of time before nausea was reported is shown in dark gray and the spectra associated with the period of time after the nausea was reported is shown in light gray.

Abnormal rhythms dominated by the slower waves of bradygastria are seen prior to the nausea report. After the report, the faster waves of tachygastria are observed as the primary abnormal rhythm. Increased tachygastria during nausea has also been shown by EGG during motion sickness on Earth.

Source: Harm DL, Sandoz GR, Stern RM. Changes in Gastric Myoelectric Activity During Space Flight. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2002 Aug; 47(8):1737-1745.

datasets.datasetName: Cell Activation
datasets.experimentTitle: Human Lymphocyte Locomotion in Microgravity
description:
This graph depicts the effect of cell activation prior to rotating-wall vessel (RWV) culture on peripheral blood lymphocyte (PBL) locomotion. PBLs were cultured in c-RPMI with 1 µg/ml anti-CD3 and 200 U/ml interleukin-2 for 10 days at 37° C. Cells were then cultured in static flasks or RWVs for an additional 48 hours. PBL locomotion assayed thereafter and compared with locomotion of non-activated lymphocytes. Data are presented as mean locomotory distance (µm) ± standard error of the mean (SEM).

Source: Unpublished data.

datasets.datasetName: Final Report: Skin Temperatures During Unaided Egress: Unsuited and While Wearing the NASA Launch and Entry or Advanced Crew Escape Suits
datasets.experimentTitle: Interaction of the Space Shuttle Launch and Entry Suit and Sustained Weightlessness on Egress Locomotion
description:
Report NASA/TM—2000–209761, Skin Temperatures During Unaided Egress: Unsuited and While Wearing the NASA Launch and Entry or Advanced Crew Escape Suits, contains final results from the skin temperature subset of measurements performed as part of DSO 331.

In this report, the following data are presented:

  • Preflight Unsuited vs. Suited Condition
  • Advanced Crew Escape Suits (ACES) vs. Launch and Entry Suit (LES)
  • A comparison was also made for the skin temperatures at four stages of landing.
  • Comparisons were also made between preflight and postflight suited conditions.
  • Comparisons between the two suits at the arm, chest, and thigh measurement sites, and in the mean skin temperature.

datasets.datasetName: Time Course and Space Motion Sickness
datasets.experimentTitle: Clinical Characterization of Space Motion Sickness (SMS)
description:
This graph depicts the time course of symptoms for space motion sickness (SMS) and the range of symptoms that have been recorded on Shuttle crewmembers. With one exception, onset of symptoms (e.g., usually, awareness of motion sensitivity by occasionally vomiting) occurs within minutes to 1-2 hours of exposure to weightlessness. The symptoms progress in intensity over a period of hours to a plateau, which, for a given condition remains stable. There are typically both head (motion sensitivity, malaise, somnolence, lethargy, etc.) and gut (anorexia, vomiting, and nausea) symptoms, although one or the other may predominate.

A small subset of crewmembers took medications to prevent SMS only to have the symptoms appear after discontinuation of the medication.

Source: Thornton WE, Moore TP, Pool SL, and Vanderploeg J. Clinical characterization and etiology of space motion sickness. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. 1987 September; 58(9 Pt 2):A1-8.

datasets.datasetName: Listing of In-flight SMS Studies
datasets.experimentTitle: Clinical Characterization of Space Motion Sickness (SMS)
description:
This table contains a listing of space motion sickness (SMS) studies. Regular and repeated, preflight, in-flight, and postflight examinations of 10 crewmembers, 4 of whom had SMS, were made by two physicians who had been flown for the study of SMS on two flights. Close observation of seven additional subjects, four with SMS, were also made on ground and in flight by the same physicians on a second flight. Specific postflight debriefings were conducted by the investigator on a total of 32 subjects, 16 who had SMS, and who had participated in some phase of this study. In addition, informal discussions were held on the subject by the investigator with every person flying on Shuttle except some crewmembers of SL-1 and D-1 missions.

Source: Thornton WE, Moore TP, Pool SL, and Vanderploeg J. Clinical characterization and etiology of space motion sickness. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. 1987 September; 58(9 Pt 2):A1-8.

datasets.datasetName: Schematic Representation of Inflight Experiment Session
datasets.experimentTitle: Changes in Total Body Water During Space Flight
description:
This graph depicts the protocol for a typical measurement (Figure 2 in referenced publication). The measurements were initiated immediately after a sleep cycle with the crewmember in a fasted state. After the collection of background samples, the dose was consumed followed by at least 50 mL of fruit juice or galley water. The subject was allowed to consume a light breakfast 30 minutes after dose administration and was requested to abstain from caffeine-containing beverages for the duration of the experiment. All food consumed during the experiment was recorded on a log sheet.

Source: Leach CS, Inners, DL, and Charles, JB. Changes in Total Body Water During Spaceflight. Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 1991; 31: 1001-1006.

description:

The present calculation seems to agree well with the experiment except for the low y (below 10 keV/µm) region for which contributions from indirect delta rays events are not yet considered.

Source: Shinn JL, Dadwar GD, Xaposos MA, and Wilson JW. An analysis of energy deposition in a tissue equivalent proportional counter onboard the space shuttle. Radiation Measurements. 1999. Feb; 30(1):19-28.

datasets.datasetName: STS-31 TEPC Dose Rates in B-L Coordinates
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph displays the late April 1990 position of the Inner Belt projection in the SAA displayed in the B-L coordinate system. The numbers along the contours indicate dose rate in millirads/minute. The region containing contours is rather small in extent because of the limited latitudinal excursion of the orbiter during STS-31. The peak of the radiation belt seen in the SAA, occurs at L= 1.3 during a geomagnetically relatively quiet period. Note the limited regions of the B-L space sampled during that mission.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: SAA as seen by the STS-40 Mission
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts a contour map of the dose rate in longitude-latitude coordinates. The SAA stands out as a dose maximum with a center at about -32 degrees longitude and -36 degrees latitude. However, there is a clear indication of another peak at about +10 degrees longitude and below -39 degrees latitude. Note the appearance of the second radiation belt.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: B-L Plot of the SAA as seen by STS-48
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts the B-L plot of the SAA as seen by STS-48 including the second belt which has by now moved to L= 1.8. Viewing this in the B-L coordinate system as shown in this graph, the second belt at L= 1.8 is clearly visible. This suggests a radically inward motion of the belt over a period of time. The main belt now appears at L= 1.26 which probably is within the digitization error of the contouring program.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate Measured on Two Passes Through the SAA
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts the dose rate measured on two passes through the SAA with the TEPC responding mainly to a westward flux and one pass when it was responding mainly to an eastward flux. The ratio of the peaks is approximately 1.4. This should be viewed only as a qualitative measure of the east - west asymmetry because of the broad directional response of the detector due to the shuttle mass distribution and the uncertainties in the exact orientation of the shuttle.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: STS-37 Dose Rates in B-L Coordinates
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts the B-L plot for STS-37 a year later, at the beginning of April 1991. The intensity peak occurs at L= 1.25, a slight change perhaps associated with the aftermath of the March 24, 1991 storm. Since both STS-31 and STS-37 had the same low orbital inclination, though the latter flew at a lower altitude, the B-L space sampled is similar but even more restricted for STS-37.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: STS-40 Dose Rate in B-L Coordinates
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts the function of B and L coordinates, The SAA is at L= 1.3 though spread to L=.1.5, and the second peak is at L=.2.0. This flight occurred during a very disturbed period with Kp reaching 9 and the Dst going down to 219. Note the second belt at L=2.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: Dose Rate on STS-31 at 617 km Altitude
datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts the dose rate in mrad per minute on STS-31 at 617 km altitude. The heart of the anomaly is not accessible because of the low inclination of the orbit. The graph also shows a contour plot of dose rate in a portion of the SAA as seen by the TEPC aboard STS-31. This diagram presents the average of all passes through the SAA for that mission and was produced without regard for spacecraft orientation. Note the center of the anomaly is south of the 28.5 degree parallel.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.experimentTitle: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
description:
This graph depicts a complete picture of the SAA including the second belt as seen by STS-48. Since the STS-48 orbital inclination was -57 degrees, the spacecraft covered all of the SAA during flight. This is shown in the graph. The second belt also stands out clearly with its center at -10 degrees longitude and -40 degrees latitude.

Source: Konradi A, Badwar GD, and Braby LA. Recent space shuttle observations of the South Atlantic Anomaly and the radiation belt models. Advances in Space Research. 1994. Oct; 14(10):911-21.

datasets.datasetName: Changes in Strength of the Trunk
datasets.experimentTitle: The Evaluation of Concentric and Eccentric Skeletal Muscle Contractions Following Space Flight
description:
This graph represents changes in strength of the trunk on landing day in those subjects who exercised on a treadmill during flight versus those who did not. Although the inflight exercise group had lost more strength at landing, when the changes were expressed as percentages, preflight strength in trunk flexion and extension was substantially greater in the exercising group. These results imply that treadmill exercise did not prevent decrements in trunk strength after 9-11 days of space flight, and that preservation of muscle integrity may be limited to only those muscles exercised.

Source: Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP) Final Report

datasets.datasetName: Acrophases and Phase Delays
datasets.experimentTitle: Assessment of Circadian Shifting in Astronauts by Bright Light
description:
This Excel file contains acrophases (the time at which the peak of a rhythm occurs) and phase delays calculated before and after a 7-day bright-light/sleep-shifting protocol in 8 subjects. The cortisol and melatonin acrophases in the test group were within 2.5 hours of those for the control group.

Source: Whitson PA, Putcha L, Chen YM, and Baker E. Melatonin and cortisol assessment of circadian shifts in astronauts before flight. Journal of Pineal Research. 1995. April; 18(3):141-7.

datasets.datasetName: Circadian Shifting Before Space Flight
datasets.experimentTitle: Assessment of Circadian Shifting in Astronauts by Bright Light
description:
This graph depicts circadian-shifting protocols (A, B, and C) followed by astronauts (N=8) before launch. Open squares indicate exposure to bright light (>7,000 lux); hatched squares indicate darkness, dim light, or dark goggles; filled squares indicate sleeping period. L-n is the number of days before launch. These protocols were developed by Drs. K. Stewart and C. Eastman of Rush University College of Medicine under contract to NASA. Subjects were instructed either to sleep in the daytime (1000 to 1800) (Protocol A, N=3) or to go to bed progressively later and sleep later over a 6-day period (Protocols B and C) (N=3 and N=2, respectively). All subjects were exposed to bright light (7,000-12,000 lux) for 2-6 hours daily before their scheduled sleep periods.

Source: Whitson PA, Putcha L, Chen YM, and Baker E. Melatonin and cortisol assessment of circadian shifts in astronauts before flight. Journal of Pineal Research. 1995. April; 18(3):141-7.

datasets.datasetName: Melatonin Sulfate Rhythm
datasets.experimentTitle: Assessment of Circadian Shifting in Astronauts by Bright Light
description:
This graph depicts the melatonin sulfate rhythm in urine samples from one subject in the Protocol A group during the baseline and treatment periods. The shaded areas indicate the dark portion of the light -dark cycle, irrespective of the treatment protocol. Protocol A changed from 0300-0400 to 1500-2300 after only 3 days of treatment. The more gradual change in melatonin acrophase (the time at which the peak of a rhythm occurs) of the subjects who followed Protocols B (N=3) or C (N=2) paralleled the more gradual changes in their sleep-wake times.

Source: Whitson PA, Putcha L, Chen YM, and Baker E. Melatonin and cortisol assessment of circadian shifts in astronauts before flight. Journal of Pineal Research. 1995. April; 18(3):141-7.

datasets.datasetName: Melatonin and Cortisol Rhythms
datasets.experimentTitle: Assessment of Circadian Shifting in Astronauts by Bright Light
description:
This graph depicts melatonin and cortisol rhythms in untreated control subjects. Panels A and B reflect melatonin or melatonin sulfate concentrations in saliva or urine, respectively. Cortisol rhythms are shown in Panel C (saliva) and Panel D (urine). Points are means, and error bars SEM, for 15 subjects (14 in Panel A). Normal melatonin rhythms were confirmed in 14 of the 15 control subjects; melatonin concentrations in the saliva of the 15th subject did not change over the course of the day. Melatonin and melatonin sulfate concentrations in saliva and urine, respectively, were low during the day, began to increase at 1800, peaked after midnight, and began to decrease at dawn (panels A and B). Cosinor analysis indicated that the melatonin acrophase (the time at which the peak of a rhythm occurs) was 0130 (saliva) and the melatonin-sulfate acrophase was 0230 (urine).

Cortisol concentrations in the control subjects followed a classic diurnal pattern (panels C and D), with concentrations lowest at 2000, remaining low until an abrupt peak around 0600, and decreasing thereafter. Cosinor analysis indicated cortisol acrophases of 0700 (saliva) and 0730 (urine). Individual variations in cortisol concentration were greater than those for melatonin.

Source: Whitson PA, Putcha L, Chen YM, and Baker E. Melatonin and cortisol assessment of circadian shifts in astronauts before flight. Journal of Pineal Research. 1995. April; 18(3):141-7.

datasets.datasetName: Cardiac Measures for Control Group
datasets.experimentTitle: Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension
description:
This graph depicts mean preflight (black circles, n = 5) and landing day (white circles, n = 5) heart rate, stroke volume, and total peripheral resistance measurements during supine rest and 10 minutes of tilt/stand for the control flight group (A) during the DSO 503S study. Bars represent SEM; * p = 0.001; † p = 0.056. There were no statistically significant differences between BP or cardiac output. No subject experienced hypotension or presyncope during any test. Hemodynamic responses were very similar between flights. Of note, however, is that mean postflight upright heart rate was significantly higher than the preflight baseline for the control flight (p = 0.001), but was not after the Midodrine flight (p = 0.185) compared with their respective preflight upright heart rates. Importantly, Midodrine did not result in significantly increased supine or upright blood pressure. Additionally, supine stroke volume (p = 0.056) tended to be higher after Midodrine, compared with preflight.

Source: Platts SH, Ziegler MG, Waters WW, and Meck JV. Hemodynamic effects of midodrine after spaceflight in astronauts without orthostatic hypotension. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. 2006;77:429-433.

datasets.datasetName: Midodrine as a Countermeasure to Orthostatic Hypotension Immediately after Space Shuttle Landing
datasets.experimentTitle: Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension
description:
This report represents midodrine data as a preventative for post-space flight orthostatic intolerance when testing is conducted in a controlled laboratory setting within 2-4 hours after Space Shuttle landing.
FIGURE 1. The probability of completing a 10-minute 80° head-up tilt test in the laboratory before space flight (L-10, solid line) was not different (p=0.17) than the probability of completing a tilt test on landing day (R+0, dashed line) in the Crew Transport Vehicle in five astronauts.
FIGURE 2. Change in heart rate (HR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), stroke volume (SV), cardiac output (CO), and total peripheral resistance (TPR) from last minute of supine rest to the last minute of tilt in the laboratory before flight (L-10) and on landing day (R+0) in the Crew Transport Vehicle. *Significantly different than L-10 (p<0.05).
TABLE I. Hemodynamic variables during the last minute of supine rest and at tilt test termination.

Source: Platts SH, Stenger MB, Ribeiro LC, Lee SMC. Midodrine as a Countermeasure to Orthostatic Hypotension Immediately After Space Shuttle Landing. Johnson Space Center. Report JSC-CN-19685.

description:
The graphs show hemodynamic responses to midodrine ingestion before and after space flight. Orthostatic landing occurred approximately 1 hour after midodrine ingestion. Midodrine was given 2 hours after landing. Phase 1 data represents 5 male non-presyncopal subjects. Phase 2 data is preliminary and represents 4 of 10 subjects completed to date. Two subjects developed presyncopal symptoms on landing day.

Source: Stenger MB, Stein SP, Meck JV, Platts SH. Midodrine as a Countermeasure for Post-Spaceflight Orthostatic Hypotension. Human Research Program Investigators' Workshop, 4-6 Feb. 2008, League City, TX, United States.[NTRS].

datasets.datasetName: Spatial Orientation Schematic Drawing
datasets.experimentTitle: Visual-Vestibular Integration
description:
This is a schematic drawing of a stimulus and response make-up of spatial orientation with neural substrate. Perception of spatial orientation is determined by integrating information from several sensory modalities. This involves higher levels of processing within the central nervous system that control eye movements, locomotion, and stable posture. Space flight operational problems occur when responses to the incorrectly perceived spatial orientation are compensatory in nature. Neuroscience investigations were conducted in conjunction with U. S. Space Shuttle flights to evaluate possible changes in the ability of an astronaut to land the Shuttle or effectively perform an emergency post-landing egress following microgravity adaptation during space flights of variable length.

Source: Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP) Final Report 1989-1995.

datasets.datasetName: Body weight

description:
This graph contains preflight and landing day body weights (A), plasma volume index (B), and red blood cell volume index (C) for astronauts in the DSO 621 study. Body weight [82.0 ± 2.4 (preflight) to 79.9 ± 2.5 kg (landing day), p = 0.51, placebo; 74.0 ± 2.5 (preflight) to 71.5 ± 2.1 kg (landing day), p = 0.63, fludrocortisone] showed no significant day or treatment effect, but the fludrocortisones group was almost significantly smaller than the placebo group (p = 0.061, preflight; p = 0.051, landing day). Of the 25 astronauts studied, 23 had decreased body weight on landing day. * p < 0.05 vs. preflight.

These observations point to the need for active detectors onboard the International Space Station for monitoring and for using directional trapped belt models for dose rate predictions.

datasets.datasetName: Neutron Dose and Dose Equivalent Rates in the Shuttle Middeck Locker

description:
This Excel file summarizes all of the dose and dose equivalent calculations. The quality factor for the neutrons is 8-9, much higher than either the trapped or galactic cosmic particles. It should also be noted that the neutron dose was computed for slightly different energy ranges in each flight, and that the shielding material in the middeck was not always the same. For comparison, the average charged-particle crew dose rate (AD) measured by TLD-I00 detectors is also given. In terms of absorbed dose rate, the average neutron contribution is approximately 9%. Using the average quality factor (ICRP-26) measured by a TEPC on STS-57 and STS-94, crew absorbed dose rates, AD, were converted to crew charged-particle dose equivalent rates, HD.

Source: Badhwar GD, Kushin VV, Akatov YuA, and Myltseva VA. Effects of trapped proton flux anisotropy on dose rates in low Earth orbit. Radiation Measurements. 1999; June 30 (3): 415-426.

The detector was activated on the second day of the flight and operated for 4.35 days. For roughly the first two days of its operations (Region A: MET < 4500 min), the peak dose rate was about 6 µGY/min and dropped to 2 µGy/min for the next two days (Region B; 4500 < MET < 7500 min) and then returned to the 6 µGy/min after this time period.

Source: Badhwar GD, Kushin VV, Akatov YuA, and Myltseva VA. Effects of trapped proton flux anisotropy on dose rates in low Earth orbit. Radiation Measurements. 1999; June 30 (3): 415-426.
