datasets.datasetName: Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center
datasets.experimentTitle: Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center
description:
The Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center is the international repository of technical data, information, and reports related to human existence in stressful environments in aerospace, under water, and Earth atmosphere. The Data Center's establishment in close relation with the Institute for Environmental Medicine enables collaborative retrieval, analysis, and modeling of physical and respiratory environment-relevant information concerning: tolerance of human organs to oxygen poisoning, respiratory and pulmonary effects, physical work capability, narcotic influences and mental performance, speech capability, hydrostatic effects, thermal effects, decompression sickness and isobaric counter-diffusion gas lesion diseases, and therapy of decompression sickness generated in extreme environments, working and shallow diving, and manned aerospace activity.

The present data system plans involve continuing to provide a mechanism for acquiring new information and integrating it with data already obtained. This allows continuing development of new analytic methods for improvement in human capability, safety in environmental extremes, and applications to clinical therapy situations.

The Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center website offers access to the data center's extensive catalog of reports and technical publications, encompassing periods prior to current Medline or other computer searchable bibliographical systems.

The data center also provides access to much of the past 50 years of diving decompression methods and concepts generated internationally by naval, industrial and university aegis. The predictive studies section of the website represents conjoined investigations by individual scientists, associated laboratories, and collaborating national agencies. A central purpose is to obtain concurrent measurements of multiple physiologic effects and recovery, in response to graded degrees and durations of imposed specific environmental stresses.

Such functions provide a living and growing archive of hard data used as a basis for direct support of national and international agencies in design of new programs or research, and especially for the integration and quantitative predictive modeling of methods for describing human physiologic tolerance and performance capabilities. The predictive models are used as practical for application to development of new procedures, to improve safety and capability in adverse environmental situations. It has been the basis for continuing scientific advisory functions to NASA, the Navy and other federal agencies, universities, and industry from its origins to the present.

datasets.datasetName: Resistance exercise as a countermeasure to disuse-induced bone loss
datasets.experimentTitle: Resistance Exercise as a Countermeasure to Disuse-induced Bone Loss
description:
This represents the final publication of results for this experiment. During spaceflight, skeletal unloading results in loss of bone mineral density (BMD). This occurs primarily in the spine and lower body regions. This loss of skeletal mass could prove hazardous to astronauts on flights of long duration. In this study, intense resistance exercise was used to test whether a training regimen would prevent the loss of BMD that accompanies disuse. Nine subjects (5 men, 4 women) participated in a supine maximal resistance exercise training program during 17 wk of horizontal bed rest. These subjects were compared with 18 control subjects (13 men, 5 women) who followed the same bed rest protocol without exercise. Determination of treatment effect was based on measures of BMD, bone metabolism markers, and calcium balance obtained before, during, and after bed rest. Exercisers and controls had significantly (P < 0.05) different means, represented by the respective following percent changes: lumbar spine BMD, +3% vs. -1%; total hip BMD, +1% vs. -3%; calcaneus BMD, +1% vs. -9%; pelvis BMD, -0.5% vs. -3%; total body BMD, 0% vs. -1%; bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, +64% vs. 0%; alkaline phosphatase, +31% vs. +5%; osteocalcin, +43% vs. +10%; 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D, +12% vs. -15%; parathyroid hormone intact molecule, +18% vs. -25%; and serum and ionized calcium, -1% vs. +1%. The difference in net calcium balance was also significant (+21 mg/day vs. -199 mg/day, exercise vs. control). The gastrocnemius and soleus muscle volumes decreased significantly in the exercise group, but the loss was significantly less than observed in the control group. The results indicate that resistance exercise had a positive treatment effect and thus might be useful as a countermeasure to prevent the deleterious skeletal changes associated with long-duration spaceflight.

Source: Shackelford LC, LeBlanc AD, Driscoll TB, Evans HJ, Rianon NJ, Smith SM, Spector E, Feeback DL, Lai D. Resistance exercise as a countermeasure to disuse-induced bone loss. J Appl Physiol (1985). 2004 Jul;97(1):119-29.

datasets.datasetName: Alendronate countermeasure results
datasets.experimentTitle: Resistance Exercise as a Countermeasure to Disuse-induced Bone Loss
description:
This article represents the summarized results of the 17 week horizontal bedrest study. Microgravity, similar to disuse immobilization on earth, causes rapid bone loss. This loss is believed to be an adaptive response to the reduced musculoskeletal forces in space and occurs gradually enough that changes occurring during short duration space flight are not a concern. Bone loss, however, will be a major impediment for long duration missions if effective countermeasures are not developed and implemented. Bed rest is used to simulate the reduced mechanical forces in humans and was used to test the hypothesis that oral alendronate would reduce the effects of long duration (17 weeks) inactivity on bone. Eight male subjects were given daily oral doses of alendronate during 17 weeks of horizontal bed rest and compared with 13 male control subjects not given the drug. Efficacy was evaluated based on measurements of bone markers, calcium balance and bone density performed before, during and after the bed rest. The results show that oral alendronate attenuates most of the characteristic changes in bone that are associated with long duration bed rest and presumably space flight.

Source: LeBlanc AD, Driscol TB, Shackelford LC, Evans HJ, Rianon NJ, Smith SM, Feeback DL, Lai D. Alendronate as an effective countermeasure to disuse induced bone loss. J Musculoskelet Neuronal Interact. 2002 Jun;2(4):335-43.

datasets.datasetName: First Floor Dosimeter Readings
datasets.experimentTitle: Acoustic Noise During the Phase III Chamber Test
description:
The first table shows the number of minutes recorded at each decibel level during sound measurement of the first floor of the chamber. The percentage of total recording time is given for each decibel level. The number of hours at each decibel level are also shown. This table is then plotted in the second graph.

The small table under the first table breaks down the data into decibel ranges, enabling the viewer to assess how long each decibel range was experienced in the chamber. No time was spent with decibels under sixty; the entire recording time measured sixty decibels and up. Nearly ninety percent of the 24-hour time spent monitoring was recorded at sixty to seventy decibels. Approximately ten percent of the monitoring time was recorded at seventy to eighty decibels, and no time was recorded at eighty decibels or above.

The first graph shows the distribution of decibels of sound across the hours of the day that was measured. As expected, the lowest noise levels occurred during the early morning hours and were relatively consistent during sleeping hours.

The second graph plots the time in minutes spent at each decibel level. The numbers at the top of the bars are the number of minutes at that bar decibel value. This graph reflects the data in the first table above it.

The bottom table shows the decibel reading at each minute recorded during the 24-hour recording period.

Source: Foley T. Unpublished data.

datasets.datasetName: Duration of Floor Use and Time
datasets.experimentTitle: Sociokinetic Analysis as a Tool for Optimization of Environmental Design
description:
This figure shows a temporal analysis which averages the usage over all three weeks. The rates of use for the airlock and Level Two appear to be similar. Because of the exercise function in the airlock, its use by only a single crewmember at a time was extended throughout the waking day with small peaks between 08:00 and 10:00 and between 18:00 and 20:00 as personnel used it for exercise. Level Two usage, however, was almost exclusively in 20-second increments steadily throughout the day û in other words, the amount of time it took for a person to traverse the Level Two landing on the stair while in transit between Levels One and Three. Occasionally, crewmembers would spend slightly larger blocks of time in Level Two in order to check or maintain equipment, but the greatest percentage of use stems from the transit function which was more or less constant throughout the day.

The primary focuses of this ground-based experiment were to study and monitor the four subject's daily routines and behavior patterns in the enclosed habitat and apply design techniques to those for long duration space flight missions.

datasets.datasetName: Aerobic Exercise Countermeasure Protocol
datasets.experimentTitle: Exercise Countermeasures Demonstration Projects During The Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Phases IIa and III
description:
Figure shows the protocol used during the aerobic exercise (cycle ergometer) countermeasure for both Phase Iia and Phase III of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Project. The exercise protocol began with a warm-up period of seven minutes at an exercise intensity equivalent to 40% VO2pk. Thereafter, the exercise intensity alternated in 2-minute intervals between 40% VO2pk and 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, and 80% VO2pk. This interval training period was then followed by five minutes of exercise cool-down at 40% VO2pk.

Source: Lee SMC, Guilliams ME, Schneider SM. Aerobic Exercise Countermeasure Protocol Exercise Countermeasures Demonstration Projects During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Phases Iia and III. In : Lane HW, Sauer RL, and Feeback DL, eds. Isolation: NASA Experiments in Closed-Environment Living. American Astronautical Society Science and Technology Series; Vol 104. San Diego, CA. datasets.datasetName: Results from the Artificial Gravity Study
datasets.experimentTitle: Clinical Nutritional Assessment (Flight Analog)
parameters: Beta carotene equivalents derived from provitamin A carotenoids
C terminal telopeptide CTX in urine
Cholesterol to Saturated Fatty Acid Index
gamma linolinec acid GLA in urine
description: Spaceflight and bed rest models of microgravity have profound effects on physiological systems, including the cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and immune systems. These effects can be exacerbated by suboptimal nutrient status, and therefore it is critical to monitor nutritional status when evaluating countermeasures to mitigate negative effects of spaceflight. As part of a larger study to investigate the usefulness of artificial gravity as a countermeasure for musculoskeletal and cardiovascular deficits during bed rest, we tested the hypothesis that artificial gravity would have an effect on some aspects of nutritional status. Dietary intake was recorded daily before, during, and after 21 days of bed rest with artificial gravity (n = 8) or bed rest alone (n = 7). We examined body composition, hematology, general blood chemistry, markers of oxidative damage, and blood levels of selected vitamins and minerals before, during, and after the bed rest period. Several indicators of vitamin status changed in response to diet changes: serum alpha- and gamma-tocopherol and urinary 4-pyridoxic acid decreased (P < 0.001) and plasma beta-carotene increased (P < 0.001) in both groups during bed rest compared with before bed rest. A decrease in hematocrit (P < 0.001) after bed rest was accompanied by a decrease in transferrin (P < 0.001), but transferrin receptors were not changed. These data provide evidence that artificial gravity itself does not negatively affect nutritional status during bed rest. Likewise, artificial gravity has no protective effect on nutritional status during bed rest.

datasets.datasetName: Sweat Calcium Loss in the Bed Rest Exercise Subjects
datasets.experimentTitle: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
description:
Data for five exercise test subjects on bed rest are shown in this table. Data from exercise and non-exercise days are shown. No statistically significant differences were detected between exercise and non-exercise days and between two consecutive exercise days for the same individual. The lack of difference between exercise and non-exercise days may be attributed to the cool environment in which the exercise was performed and, possibly, the fact that resistive exercise was performed rather than aerobic. Calcium loss is given in milligrams. Three sites on the body, the upper arm, chest and back, were sampled using a skin patch. The data in this table are from averages of two consecutive exercise days, or two non-exercise days one week apart. The mean and standard error were calculated for each grouping.

In: Rianon N, Feeback D, Wood R, Driscoll T, Shackelford L, LeBlanc A. Monitoring Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches. Calcified Tissue International. 2003;72:694-697.

datasets.datasetName: Sweat Calcium Loss Before Bed Rest
datasets.experimentTitle: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
description:
This table shows the loss of calcium in sweat of twelve test subjects. Calcium loss is given in milligrams. Three sites on the body, the upper arm, chest and back, were sampled using a skin patch. Statistically significant effects were detected for back versus arm and back versus chest but not chest versus arm. The subjects wore the skin patch on two consecutive days but no differences were observed between the days. Each of the three sites on the body was sampled in duplicate but no differences were observed between the duplicates for any of the sites. Of the twelve subjects, three participated in resistive exercise and nine did not exercise. All subject results were pooled and averaged to produce the data in this table.

In: Rianon N, Feeback D, Wood R, Driscoll T, Shackelford L, LeBlanc A. Monitoring Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches. Calcified Tissue International. 2003;72:694-697.

datasets.datasetName: Hypercortisolemia alters muscle protein anabolism following ingestion of essential amino acids
datasets.experimentTitle: Nutritional Intervention to Improve Muscle Protein Metabolism during Stress
description:
This publication represents the final report for this investigation. Abstract: Debilitating injury is accompanied by hypercortisolemia, muscle wasting, and disruption of the normal anabolic response to food. We sought to determine whether acute hypercortisolemia alters muscle protein metabolism following ingestion of a potent anabolic stimulus: essential amino acids (EAA). A 27-h infusion (80 µg · kg-1 · h-1) of hydrocortisone sodium succinate mimicked cortisol (C) levels accompanying severe injury (>30 µg/dl), (C + AA;n = 6). The control group (AA) received intravenous saline (n = 6). Femoral arteriovenous blood samples and muscle biopsies were obtained during a primed (2.0 µmol/kg) constant infusion (0.05 µmol · kg-1 · min-1) ofl-[ring-2H5]phenylalanine before and after ingestion of 15 g of EAA. Hypercortisolemia [36.5 ± 2.1 (C + AA) vs. 9.0 ± 1.0 µg/dl (AA)] increased postabsorptive arterial, venous, and muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations. Hypercortisolemia also increased postabsorptive and post-EAA insulin concentrations. Net protein balance was blunted (40% lower) following EAA ingestion but remained positive for a greater period of time (60 vs. 180 min) in the C + AA group. Thus, although differences in protein metabolism were evident, EAA ingestion improved muscle protein anabolism during acute hypercortisolemia and may help minimize muscle loss following debilitating injury.

Source: Paddon-Jones D, Sheffield-Moore M, Creson DL, Sanford AP, Wolf SE, Wolfe RR, Ferrando AA. Hypercortisolemia alters muscle protein anabolism following ingestion of essential amino acids. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2003 May;28(5):E946-53.

description:
This table shows rat body weight, body composition and biochemical markers of bone metabolism in response to three doses of Vitamin E in the diet. The lowest dose was 15 international units. The middle dose was 75 international units, and the highest dose was 500 international units. Body weight is given in grams. Body composition is given in grams of fat and lean body mass. The serum analysis included alkaline phosphatase (ALP), a marker of bone formation, and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), a marker of bone resorption. The ALP activity is given in microkatals per liter, a measure of catalytic activity. The statistical significance of the data can be seen in the last three columns of the table.

In: Smith BJ, Lucas EA, Turner RT, Evans GL, Lerner MR, Brackett DJ, Stoecker BJ, Arjmandi BH. Vitamin E provides protection for bone in mature hindlimb unloaded male rats. Calcified Tissue International. 2004 Mar.

Each point represents the average DQS from about 100 wave files in each of the eight data sessions (data collection oportunities) in each diver. datasets.datasetName: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria, Survival Analysis Data
datasets.experimentTitle: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria
description:
Test of resistance to different agents with treatment of radiation, or hydrogen peroxide or acid after growth under normal gravity (NG) and LSMMG. For survival data LHM4 strain was used as this is a derivative of strain 1218R. A plasmid is incorporated into the genome that encodes red fluorescent protein and kanamycin resistance. Bacteria were grown and treated according to Abshire et al NOJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi:10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38.

LHM4 were removed from the HARV and the OD600 measured in a sample after disaggregation. Bacteria were in exponential phase (OD600 0.09-0.2). For radiation and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) studies, bacteria were centrifuged and washed in PBS containing 0.2% Tween 80 (Tw-PBS) , before resuspension at OD600 ~0.2 in Tw-PBS. Two samples (200 µl in a sealed tube) were prepared for each time point or dose. One sample was treated (1-4 hours) with 5 mM H2O2 at 30°C or with ? radiation (100-400 Gy) at room temperature. The second sample was not treated and was used as the control to determine the CFU/ ml at zero treatment at the time point. A similar method was used to treat the bacteria with acid. The bacteria were centrifuged and resuspended at OD600 ~0.2 in growth medium (control) or growth medium at pH 3.5. 1 M citric acid was added to the medium to reach pH 3.5. Once the bacteria were resuspended, the pH was checked using pH paper. The control and acid-treated samples were incubated at 30°C for 1-4 hours. After all treatment regimens, bacteria were disaggregated and diluted as described above and grown on three plates containing solid medium. Bacteria were incubated at 30°C for 7-10 days and the CFU/ ml calculated for each control and treated sample. Survival was calculated by:% Survival = Avg CFU/ ml of treated culture x 100, Avg CFU/ ml of control culture

The survival data were compared by calculating the area under the curve for each data set using the Trapezoidal Rule, and the Student T test was used to compare the values. These statistical analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Inc. Gary, NC).

Time period of collection range from February 3, 2014 to February 17, 2015.

datasets.datasetName: S. mutans HARV metabolic assays
datasets.experimentTitle: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
description:
Dataset represents the HARV metabolomics assays in the form of graphs and spreadsheets. Detailed data descriptions can be found below and included with each figure legend (or notes in spreadsheets). Treatment details follow the dataset description.

Figure 1. Principle Component Analysis (PCA) of cellular (A) and supernatant (B) metabolites. Values on X and Y axis labels = % of the total eigen values.

For this experiment, overnight S. mutans cultures were used to inoculate 350 ml sterile BM containing 11mM glucose and 10mM sucrose to an approximate OD600 = 0.06/ml. 1 ml was withdrawn to measure the t = 0 OD600, pH, and CFU/ml. The remaining inoculum volume was then immediately used to fill 6 × 50 ml disposable HARVs. A sterile media control was also collected at the beginning of each experiment and stored at -80 °C for metabolomics analysis. For each experiment, three simulated microgravity and three normal gravity HARV cultures were grown in parallel at 37 °C, 5% CO2 as described for the end-point growth curve analysis. For each experiment, one simulated microgravity and one normal gravity HARV were each harvested at t = 4, t = 8 h, and t = 24 h growth. After harvesting, 34 ml of each t = 4, 8, and 24 h HARV culture was centrifuged at 3000 RPM, 4 °C for 20 min and immediately placed on ice. 1ml of culture supernatant was removed from each centrifuged sample, transferred to 1.5 ml tubes, and immediately frozen at -80 °C. The remaining culture supernatants were decanted and cell pellets immediately frozen at -80 °C. Extraction of metabolites and all metabolomics analyses (including statistics) were performed by Metabolon, Inc. (Durham, NC) methods. Detailed extraction methods, statistical analysis, etc. is in the Metabolon final report

datasets.datasetName: S. mutans HARV growth asssays (planktonic)
datasets.experimentTitle: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
description:
Dataset represents the HARV growth assays in the form of graphs and images. Detailed data descriptions can be found below and included with each figure legend. Treatment details follow the dataset description.

Figure 1: End-point growth curve analysis of S. mutans simulated microgravity and normal gravity HARV cultures. Simulated microgravity (dark grey bars) and normal gravity (light grey bars) HARV end-point growth was measured by serial dilution and CFU/ml plating at t = 0 (time of inoculation; average of n=4 independent experiments), and t= 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and 48 hours’ post- inoculation (average of n=2 independent experiments per time point per growth condition). The vertical dotted line on the graph indicates that the t=24 and 48-hour data were obtained in a separate experimental run from the t=4, 6, 8, and 12-hour time points. Error bars = standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 2: Continuous growth curve analysis of S. mutans simulated microgravity and normal gravity HARV cultures. Each simulated microgravity (triangles) and normal gravity (circles) HARV growth curve was performed in biofilm media for 24 hours at 37°C and 5% CO2. HARVs were sampled for serial dilution and CFU/ml determination at t = 0 (time of inoculation), 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours’ post-inoculation, as described in Materials and Methods. Data represent n=3 independent experiments per growth condition, error bars = standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 3: OD600 (A), CFU/ml (B), and pH (C) data corresponding to end-point S. mutans microgravity and normal gravity HARV cultures harvested for metabolomics (t=4, 8, and 24 hours’ growth) and for RNA-seq (t=8 hours only). Data represent n=3 independent experiments per time point per growth condition. Error bars = standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 4: Representative S. mutans HARVs grown for 8 hours, 30 RPM, in BM under either simulated microgravity (Left) or normal gravity (Right) conditions. Note the structural differences of the self-aggregating bacterial cells under each condition (indicated by arrows).

Figure 5: Diagrams of Disposable Vessel Rotary Cell Culture Systems used to simulate microgravity (A; HARV rotated on an axis perpendicular to gravitational vector) and normal gravity (B; HARV rotated on an axis parallel to gravitational vector) growth conditions

For the continuous HARV Growth Curves experiment, overnight S. mutans cultures were used to inoculate 120 ml of sterile BM containing 11 mM glucose and 10 mM sucrose to an OD600 = 0.06. This inoculum was mixed well by vigorous swirling and vortexing, and 1 ml withdrawn to measure the time-of-inoculation (t=0) CFU/ml. The remaining inoculum volume was then subjected again to vigorous swirling and vortexing and immediately used to fill 2 x 50 ml disposable HARVs as described above. Each HARV was rotated either vertically (“simulated microgravity”) or horizontally (“normal gravity”) at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 24 hours. HARVs were rotated at 30 RPM for the first 8 hours of growth, and the rotation speed of each reactor was increased to 32 RPM after 8 hours of growth to ensure that S. mutans cell aggregates did not settle to the bottom of the simulated microgravity HARV. At 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours’ post-inoculation, each HARV was removed from the incubator, vigorously agitated to evenly disperse cell clumps, and 1 ml culture was immediately removed for CFU/ml assessment. The same volume of sterile media was then added back to each HARV and air bubbles removed prior to continued growth. For CFU/ml quantification, each 1 ml sample was vortexed vigorously for at least 30 seconds to resuspend cell clumps, followed immediately by serial dilution (each tube vortexed vigorously for at least 15 seconds between each dilution) and CFU/ml determination using the track plating method.

Treatment for the HARV "End-Point" Growth Curves used overnight S. mutans cultures to inoculate 500 ml sterile BM containing 11 mM glucose and 10 mM sucrose to an approximate OD600 = 0.06/ml as described above. 1 ml was withdrawn to measure the t=0 OD600, pH, and CFU/ml. The remaining inoculum volume was then immediately used to fill 8 x 50 ml disposable HARVs. For end-point growth curve analysis at t=4, 6, 8, and 12 hours conditions, 4 simulated microgravity and 4 normal gravity HARV cultures were grown in parallel at 37°C, 5% CO2. HARVs were rotated at 30 RPM for the first 8 hours of growth, and the rotation speed of each reactor was increased to 32 RPM after 8 hours of growth. At each time point, one simulated microgravity and one normal gravity HARV were each harvested for CFU/ml, OD600, and pH measurements.

datasets.datasetName: S. mutans HARV oxidative stress assays
datasets.experimentTitle: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
description:
Dataset represents the HARV oxidative stress assays in the form of graphs. Detailed data descriptions can be found below and included with each figure legend. Treatment details follow the dataset description.

Figure 1: Cells from t=4 (A), t=8 (B), or t=16 (C) hour simulated microgravity (triangles) and normal gravity (circles) HARV cultures (n=3 independent experiments per time point per growth condition) were harvested by centrifugation and resuspended in sterile HBSS. Samples were withdrawn to determine initial CFU/ml (“t=0”), and then H2O2 was added to a final concentration of 5 mM. CFU/ml of each cell suspension was sampled at 20, 40, 60, 90, and 120 minutes post-H2O2 addition, and CFU/ml were determined. % Survival was calculated by 100 x [(t=final CFU/ml)/ (t=0 CFU/ml)]. Error bars = SEM. *Denotes statistical significance, one-tailed t-test (p< 0.05).

Treatment included normal gravity and simulated microgravity HARV (50 ml size) growth, 37ºC, 5% CO2, 30-35 RPM in Biofilm media containing glucose and sucrose. For each experiment, S. mutans 10-ml HARV cultures were grown for either 4, 8, or 16 h. For the 4 and 8 h experiments, the HARV rotation speed was 30 RPM. For the 16 h experiment, the HARV rotation speed was 30 RPM for the first 8 h of growth, and was then increased to 35 RPM to counteract sedimentation of cellular aggregates. S. mutans cultures were then harvested from each HARV vessel, transferred to a 50 ml Falcon tube, and centrifuged for 10 min at 4000 RPM. Cell pellets were resuspended in 5 ml sterile 1× Hanks Buffered Salt Solution (HBSS), and 100 µl was withdrawn from each tube and subjected to serial dilution plating as described above to enumerate CFU/ml of each cell suspension at “t = 0” (prior to H2O2 addition). H2O2 was added to each remaining 4.9 ml cell suspension to a final concentration of 5 mM, and incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2. Samples of each cell suspension were removed at 15, 30, 45, 60, and 120 min post-H2O2 addition to enumerate CFU/ml, and % survival for each sample was calculated by 100× (t = × CFU/ml/t = 0 CFU/ml).

datasets.datasetName: S. mutans HARV competence assays
datasets.experimentTitle: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
description:
Dataset represents the HARV competence assays in the form of two graphs. Detailed data descriptions can be found below and included with each figure legend. Treatment details follows the dataset description.

Figure 1: S. mutans competence phenotype assessed in simulated microgravity and normal gravity HARV cultures. Simulated microgravity and normal gravity HARV cultures, as well as a parallel static Falcon tube control culture, were each grown for 1.5 hours in biofilm media prior to addition of 2 µg pOri23 plasmid DNA. All three cultures were then grown or 2.5 more hours followed by harvest and serial dilution plating on BHI agar ± 10 µg/ml erythromycin (selective antibiotic to monitor plasmid transformation). Transformation efficiency was calculated as the percentage of transformants (CFU/ml on BHI + erythromycin) among total viable cells (CFU/ml on BHI). Data represent the average of n=3 independent experiments. Error bars =SEM.

Figure 2: Quantitative competence assay. S. mutans HARV cultures were grown for 1.5 hours in BHI containing 5% horse serum prior to addition of 2 µg plasmid DNA. HARV cultures were then grown for 2.5 more hours followed by harvest and serial dilution plating on BHI agar ± selective antibiotic. Transformation efficiency was calculated as calculated as the percentage of transformants (CFU/ml on BHI + selective antibiotic) among total viable cells (CFU/ml on BHI). Data represents the average of n=3 independent experiments. Error bars = SEM.

Treatment simulated normal gravity and simulated microgravity HARV (10 ml size) growth, 37ºC, 5% CO2, 30 RPM in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth or Biofilm media containing glucose and sucrose (as indicated in graph figure legends). HARVS were removed from rotator bases after 90 minutes growth, and 2 µg of unmethylated plasmid DNA was added to each reactor. Microgravity and normal gravity HARVs were then incubated for 2.5 h prior to serial dilution and plating of each culture on BHI agar ±10 µg/ml erythromycin (Erm; selectable antibiotic for plasmid). CFU/ml were determined after 48 h plate growth, and transformation efficiencies were calculated as the percentage of transformants (BHI-Erm CFU/ml) among the total viable cells (BHI CFU/ml). For each biofilm media experiment, a non-rotating control culture (15- ml Falcon tube containing 15 ml of S. mutans culture) was grown in parallel and assessed for competence as described above.

description:
This graph depicts the estimated survival among subjects on the nonmotorized treadmills at 6.44 (panel A), 8.05 (panel B), 9.66 (panel C), and 11.27 km-h11 (panel D). See Figure 2 in referenced publication. Each interval represents 15 seconds. Each plot is pooled across the entire sample. Survival plots were similar between treadmills at each speed, but as speed increased, the rate of failure increased. The log-rank tests revealed that the survival times for the group decreased as speed increased (p < 0.05). It should be noted that at 9.66 and 11.27 km-h1, the mean survival times were underestimated because of the large number of censored variables. There were no significant differences in survival times between treadmills.

Source: De Witt JK, Lee SM, Wilson CA, and Hagan RD. Determinants of time to fatigue during nonmotorized treadmill exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009 May; 23(3):883-90.

datasets.datasetName: Choice of Running Versus Walking on Each Treadmill for Each Speed

description:

Fourteen of 20 chose to run at 4 mph on the non-motorized treadmill. This suggests that the walk-to-run transition speed may be treadmill-modality dependent.

datasets.datasetName: Heart Rate and Arterial Pressure Response to Midodrine and Promethazine Interactions During Tilt Test
datasets.experimentTitle: Test of Interactions Between Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension and Promethazine as an Anti-emetic
description:
This table shows four points of systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and heart rate: a supine baseline before being given any medications; last supine measurement after being given midodrine or placebo midodrine; last supine measurement after promethazine or placebo promethazine administration; and last measurement of upright tilt test. This table shows that supine systolic and diastolic pressures increased significantly only in the combination group (midodrine + promethazine). Upright tilt systolic pressure decreased significantly only in the promethazine group. Upright tilt diastolic pressure did not change in all groups. In the supine position, heart rate did not change before and after being given midodrine, promethazine, or both, in all groups. However, upright tilt heart rate increased significantly in all groups.

Source: unpublished data.

datasets.datasetName: Responses to Promethazine Alone and Promethazine Plus Midodrine
datasets.experimentTitle: Test of Interactions Between Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension and Promethazine as an Anti-emetic
description:
This table contains responses to promethazine alone and promethazine plus midodrine for subjects in the ROI_MIDO_PMZ study.

*No participants experienced akathisia with double placebo use or midodrine plus placebo. † Barnes score: 0, no akathisia; 1, nonspecific inner tension and fidgety movements; 2,awareness of restlessness that is worse when required to stay still; 3, symptoms of a score of 2 plus rocking movements and distress; 4, compulsive desire to move, with obvious distress; 5, inability to remain still, with distress, insomnia, and severe anxiety.

Source: Platts SH, Shi SJ, and Meck JV. Akathisia with combined use of midodrine and promethazine. JAMA. 2006 May 3;295(17):2000-1

datasets.datasetName: Supine to Upright Changes in Cardiac Measures
datasets.experimentTitle: Test of Interactions Between Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension and Promethazine as an Anti-emetic
description:
This graph contains supine to upright changes (delta) in A) systolic pressure; B) diastolic pressure; C) heart rate; D) stroke volume; E) cardiac output; and F) total peripheral vascular resistance during control, midodrine, promethazine, and midodrine plus promethazine (combination). Significant changes were found in systolic pressure responses between control and promethazine; between midodrine and promethazine; and between midodrine and combination. Significant changes were found in diastolic pressure responses between midodrine and promethazine. Significant changes were found in cardiac output responses between control and promethazine and promethazine and combination.

Source: Shi SJ, Platts SH, Ziegler MG, and Meck JV. Effects of promethazine and midodrine on orthostatic tolerance. Aviation Space and Environmental Medicine. 2011 Jan; 82(1):9-12.

datasets.datasetName: Transmission Electron Photomicrograph of Peripheral Cytoplasm
datasets.experimentTitle: The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity
description:
This image is a transmission electron photomicrograph of peripheral cytoplasm showing free ribosomes ®, microtubules (MT), and bundles of microfibrils (MF) beneath plasma membrane. The magnification is 100,000 X.

In the 11- to 12-day old cultures filamentous mitochondria and lysosomes are decreased. Endoplasmic reticulum may be decreased and there appears to be a piling up of ribosomes around slightly dilated endoplasmic reticulum tubules. A marked increase in the number of microtubules and microfibrils is shown. As reported in: Montgomery PO, Cook JE, Reynolds RC, Paul JS, Hayflick L, Stock D, Schulz WW, Kimzey S, Thirolf RG, Rogers T, Campbell D, Murrell J. The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity. Biomedical Results of Skylab, ed. Johnson RS, Dietlein L, 1977, NASA SP 377.

datasets.datasetName: Evaluation of Physical and Chemical Changes in Pharmaceuticals Flown on Space Missions
datasets.experimentTitle: Stability of Pharmacotherapeutic Compounds
description:
This is the final published report for the pharmaceutical portion of the ISS Stability experiment. The report contains the following data:
  • Flight payload kit manifestation and return schedule. Each kit contained 33 dosage forms as 22 solid, seven semisolid, and four liquid formulations.
  • Formulation Type and Physical Variables Assessed
  • Formulations with Physical Changes after Spaceflight
  • Formulations Failing Chemical Potency Requirement
  • Degradation of amoxicillin and clavulanate in augmentin tablets
  • Degradation of ciprofloxacin and promethazine dosage forms
  • Degradation of antibiotic tablets (Cefadroxil, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin, Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole)
  • Dissolution Percent of API at USP Tolerance Time Period (Q) for Solid Formulations
  • Comparison of mean temperature (a) and relative humidity (b)conditions between ground and spaceflight
  • Comparison of cumulative radiation dose between ground and spaceflight

    Source: Du B, Daniels VR, Vaksman Z, Boyd JL, Crady C, Putcha L. Evaluation of physical and chemical changes in pharmaceuticals flown on space missions. AAPS J. 2011 Jun;13(2):299-308.
